title: Offline web apps: caching, queued writes, and conflict resolution
description: A local-first app works without a network and treats the connection as a bonus. This quiz covers service-worker caching strategies (cache-first, network-first, stale-while-revalidate), durable storage in the browser, and queueing writes made offline so you can replay them later. Then it turns to the hardest part, resolving conflicts when two clients edit the same data, with last-write-wins, version vectors, and CRDTs.

questions.title: Which caching strategy returns the cached response right away, then updates the cache in the background?
questions.description: A news feed should appear instantly on every visit, and you also want the content to be fairly fresh the *next* time it loads.

images.alt: Five steps for one offline mutation. First, apply the change optimistically, which means you must handle failure later. Second, queue the mutation locally in IndexedDB, not localStorage, with an idempotency key so a later replay is safe. Third, try to send it and let the request fail honestly. Fourth, if it fails, register a Background Sync tag so the browser replays the request when the connection returns, even after the tab closes. Fifth, if the server rejects it, roll back the optimistic change and tell the user. Four cards follow. A service worker can use only the Cache API and IndexedDB, not localStorage or document.cookie. An IndexedDB transaction commits on its own as soon as it has no pending request, so awaiting an unrelated fetch makes the next add throw TransactionInactiveError. The browser may still evict stored data unless you call navigator.storage.persist(). A true navigator.onLine only means the device has a network interface.
images.caption: Serve from the cache now, refresh it for next time.

options.text: Cache-first
Network-first
Stale-while-revalidate
Cache-only

questions.explanation:
**Stale-while-revalidate** answers from the cache right away (the "stale" part). At the same time it sends a network request, and the fresh response *replaces* the cache entry (the "revalidate" part). This load is instant, and the next one is up to date.

The other strategies work differently:

- **Cache-first** returns a cache hit and never revalidates, so it can serve stale data forever. It suits hashed, immutable assets.
- **Network-first** waits for the network and falls back to the cache only when the request fails. Use it when freshness matters more than speed.
- **Cache-only** never uses the network.

The name comes from the HTTP `Cache-Control: stale-while-revalidate` directive, which makes the same trade-off at the CDN.

questions.title: Which storage APIs can a service worker use directly?
questions.description: A service worker runs on its own worker thread. It has no `window` and no `document`, and it can't use synchronous APIs that exist only on the main thread.

images.caption: Two asynchronous stores, and no `window`.

options.text: The Cache API (`caches` / `CacheStorage`)
IndexedDB
`localStorage`
`document.cookie`

questions.explanation:
A service worker has no DOM and runs on its own thread, so it can't use anything synchronous or tied to the document:

- `localStorage` is **synchronous**, so workers don't get it.
- `document.cookie` needs a `document`, and a worker has none.

That leaves the **asynchronous** APIs that work in workers. The **Cache API** stores `Request`/`Response` pairs for offline pages, and **IndexedDB** holds structured app data and your outbox of offline mutations. This is why offline-first apps use IndexedDB and the Cache API instead of `localStorage`.

questions.title: Why does this IndexedDB write throw `TransactionInactiveError`?
questions.description:
The code should fetch some data and store it in the `outbox` object store, all in one transaction:

```js
const tx = db.transaction('outbox', 'readwrite');
const store = tx.objectStore('outbox');

const res = await fetch('/api/sync'); // await something unrelated to IndexedDB
store.add(await res.json());          // throws: TransactionInactiveError
```

images.alt: Five steps for one offline mutation. First, apply the change optimistically, which means you must handle failure later. Second, queue the mutation locally in IndexedDB, not localStorage, with an idempotency key so a later replay is safe. Third, try to send it and let the request fail honestly. Fourth, if it fails, register a Background Sync tag so the browser replays the request when the connection returns, even after the tab closes. Fifth, if the server rejects it, roll back the optimistic change and tell the user. Four cards follow. A service worker can use only the Cache API and IndexedDB, not localStorage or document.cookie. An IndexedDB transaction commits on its own as soon as it has no pending request, so awaiting an unrelated fetch makes the next add throw TransactionInactiveError. The browser may still evict stored data unless you call navigator.storage.persist(). A true navigator.onLine only means the device has a network interface.
images.caption: The transaction has already ended when `add` runs.

options.text: The transaction committed on its own while the code awaited the unrelated `fetch`, so it is no longer active when `add` runs
A `readwrite` transaction can contain only one request
`store.add` only accepts values passed through `JSON.stringify` first
IndexedDB can't store the result of `res.json()` because it is a Promise

questions.explanation:
An IndexedDB transaction stays active only while it has pending requests in the current event-loop turn. When control goes back to the event loop with nothing queued on the transaction, which is exactly what `await fetch(...)` does, the transaction **auto-commits** and becomes inactive. The later `store.add` then runs against a finished transaction and throws `TransactionInactiveError`.

To fix it, do all the other async work *first*. Then open the transaction and make every IndexedDB call inside it without awaiting anything else:

```js
const payload = await (await fetch('/api/sync')).json(); // await BEFORE the tx
const tx = db.transaction('outbox', 'readwrite');
tx.objectStore('outbox').add(payload);                   // no await in between
```

The other options are wrong. A transaction can hold many requests, `add` stores structured-cloneable values rather than JSON strings, and `await res.json()` has already resolved to a plain object. Auto-commit keeps IndexedDB transactions cheap because they never hold locks for long, but it often surprises developers used to long-lived SQL transactions.

questions.title: By default, can you count on the browser to keep the data your app writes to IndexedDB?
questions.description: Your offline-first app keeps the *only* copy of the user's unsynced work in IndexedDB.

images.alt: Five steps for one offline mutation. First, apply the change optimistically, which means you must handle failure later. Second, queue the mutation locally in IndexedDB, not localStorage, with an idempotency key so a later replay is safe. Third, try to send it and let the request fail honestly. Fourth, if it fails, register a Background Sync tag so the browser replays the request when the connection returns, even after the tab closes. Fifth, if the server rejects it, roll back the optimistic change and tell the user. Four cards follow. A service worker can use only the Cache API and IndexedDB, not localStorage or document.cookie. An IndexedDB transaction commits on its own as soon as it has no pending request, so awaiting an unrelated fetch makes the next add throw TransactionInactiveError. The browser may still evict stored data unless you call navigator.storage.persist(). A true navigator.onLine only means the device has a network interface.
images.caption: Best-effort until you ask for persistence.

options.text: No. Storage is "best-effort" by default, and the browser can evict it when disk space runs low
Yes. The data stays until the user clears the site's data
Yes, as long as the database stays under the 5 MB quota
No. The browser wipes IndexedDB every time the tab closes

questions.explanation:
Under the Storage Standard, an origin's storage is **best-effort** by default. When the device runs low on disk space, the browser may evict it, usually starting with the origins used least recently. If IndexedDB holds the *only* copy of unsynced work, request **persistent** storage with `await navigator.storage.persist()`. Once the browser grants it, it won't evict the origin on its own, and only the user can clear it. `navigator.storage.persisted()` tells you the current mode, and `navigator.storage.estimate()` shows how much space is left.

The wrong answers mix up other storage myths. The ~5 MB figure is a rough `localStorage` limit, while IndexedDB quotas are much larger and change with free disk space. Surviving a closed tab is exactly what separates IndexedDB from `sessionStorage`.

questions.title: What do you have to handle when you update the UI optimistically?
questions.description: A todo app adds a new item to local state and shows it right away, before the server confirms it was created.

images.alt: Five steps for one offline mutation. First, apply the change optimistically, which means you must handle failure later. Second, queue the mutation locally in IndexedDB, not localStorage, with an idempotency key so a later replay is safe. Third, try to send it and let the request fail honestly. Fourth, if it fails, register a Background Sync tag so the browser replays the request when the connection returns, even after the tab closes. Fifth, if the server rejects it, roll back the optimistic change and tell the user. Four cards follow. A service worker can use only the Cache API and IndexedDB, not localStorage or document.cookie. An IndexedDB transaction commits on its own as soon as it has no pending request, so awaiting an unrelated fetch makes the next add throw TransactionInactiveError. The browser may still evict stored data unless you call navigator.storage.persist(). A true navigator.onLine only means the device has a network interface.
images.caption: Step 5 undoes step 1 when the server says no.

options.text: A rollback path that undoes the local change if the server rejects it
A blocking spinner that freezes the UI until the server responds
Disabling the form until the next full page reload
Moving storage from IndexedDB to `localStorage` for speed

questions.explanation:
An optimistic update **assumes success** and changes local state right away, so the UI feels instant and keeps working offline. The cost is that you must be able to **undo** it. If the server later rejects the write because of a validation error, a conflict, or an auth failure, roll local state back to its previous value and show the error.

TanStack Query models this lifecycle directly. `onMutate` saves a snapshot of the cache and applies the optimistic change, `onError` restores the snapshot, and `onSettled` refetches to match the server. The blocking spinner is the *pessimistic* approach that optimistic UI avoids. Without a rollback path, a rejected write leaves the client showing data the server never accepted.

questions.title: What's the one-word name for the key that stops a replayed mutation from running twice?
questions.description:
When the device reconnects, your outbox replays a `POST` that may have *already* succeeded on the server before the connection dropped. To let the server recognize the retry and skip the duplicate, the client attaches a unique **______** key.

The same word describes an operation that has the same effect whether you apply it once or twice.

images.alt: Five steps for one offline mutation. First, apply the change optimistically, which means you must handle failure later. Second, queue the mutation locally in IndexedDB, not localStorage, with an idempotency key so a later replay is safe. Third, try to send it and let the request fail honestly. Fourth, if it fails, register a Background Sync tag so the browser replays the request when the connection returns, even after the tab closes. Fifth, if the server rejects it, roll back the optimistic change and tell the user. Four cards follow. A service worker can use only the Cache API and IndexedDB, not localStorage or document.cookie. An IndexedDB transaction commits on its own as soon as it has no pending request, so awaiting an unrelated fetch makes the next add throw TransactionInactiveError. The browser may still evict stored data unless you call navigator.storage.persist(). A true navigator.onLine only means the device has a network interface.
images.caption: In step 2, the key is stored with the queued mutation.

questions.explanation:
An operation is **idempotent** when running it several times has the same effect as running it once. Replaying an offline outbox is unreliable by nature, because the original request may have reached the server *before* the response was lost. So each mutation carries an **idempotency key**, a unique id the client generates (usually a UUID). The server remembers the keys it has processed. When it sees a repeat, it returns the original result instead of doing the work again. Delivery is still at-least-once, but the effect happens exactly once.

Stripe's API made this pattern popular with its `Idempotency-Key` header, so a retried charge never bills a customer twice.

questions.title: Which API holds a failed request until the browser is back online, even after the page closes?
questions.description: You want a queued message to go out as soon as the device is back online, without the user reopening the app.

images.alt: Five steps for one offline mutation. First, apply the change optimistically, which means you must handle failure later. Second, queue the mutation locally in IndexedDB, not localStorage, with an idempotency key so a later replay is safe. Third, try to send it and let the request fail honestly. Fourth, if it fails, register a Background Sync tag so the browser replays the request when the connection returns, even after the tab closes. Fifth, if the server rejects it, roll back the optimistic change and tell the user. Four cards follow. A service worker can use only the Cache API and IndexedDB, not localStorage or document.cookie. An IndexedDB transaction commits on its own as soon as it has no pending request, so awaiting an unrelated fetch makes the next add throw TransactionInactiveError. The browser may still evict stored data unless you call navigator.storage.persist(). A true navigator.onLine only means the device has a network interface.
images.caption: Step 4 still works after the tab closes.

options.text: The Background Sync API, with `registration.sync.register('tag')` and a `sync` handler in the service worker
A `setInterval` loop in the page that polls `navigator.onLine`
The page's `beforeunload` event
`storage` events that `localStorage` fires across tabs

questions.explanation:
With the **Background Sync API**, a page registers a sync tag (`await registration.sync.register('outbox')`). When the browser decides the device has connectivity, it fires a `sync` event in the **service worker**. This can happen *after the page is closed*, and if the handler rejects, the browser retries later with backoff. An offline mutation queue needs exactly this kind of replay, which doesn't depend on the page.

The wrong answers all stop working when the page closes. A `setInterval` poll and a `beforeunload` handler can't run once the tab is gone, and cross-tab `storage` events need another tab open. The polling option also relies on `navigator.onLine`, which reports only link status, not whether a server is reachable. The last question covers that.

questions.title: What is the main risk of last-write-wins conflict resolution?
questions.description: Two clients edit the same record while offline. When they sync, the write with the newer timestamp wins and the other is dropped.

images.alt: Three ways to handle concurrent edits. Last-write-wins lets one timestamp decide and silently discards the other change, and clock skew can pick the winner. Version vectors are per-node counters that detect whether two versions are causally ordered or truly concurrent. They only detect conflicts and never merge. CRDTs have a merge that is commutative, associative, and idempotent, so replicas that received the same updates converge in any order. A worked G-Counter merge follows. replicaA holds A 5, B 2, C 0, a value of 7. replicaB holds A 1, B 7, C 4, a value of 12. The element-wise maximum is A 5, B 7, C 4, so the merged value is 16. A closing line notes that converging is not the same as being right.
images.caption: In the left card, a clock decides and the other write silently disappears.

options.text: The losing write disappears silently, and clock skew can make the wrong write win
Every client must run a consensus protocol before it can write
It works only on numeric fields
It always creates a merge conflict that a person must resolve by hand

questions.explanation:
Last-write-wins (LWW) compares a timestamp or version on each write and keeps the newest one. It's simple and *fully automatic*, with no human and no coordination. That automation is also the danger. The losing write disappears with **no record and no merge**, so concurrent edits silently lose data. LWW also trusts wall-clock timestamps, and client clocks drift. A write that happened *later* in real time can carry an *earlier* timestamp and lose, or the other way around.

Systems that use LWW usually soften this with a logical or **hybrid logical clock** and a fixed tie-breaker, such as the node id, so every replica at least picks the *same* winner. When silently dropping data is unacceptable, use **version vectors** to detect concurrent edits or **CRDTs** to merge them instead of discarding one. The next two questions cover both.

questions.title: What does a version vector (vector clock) actually give you?
questions.description: Each replica keeps a map of per-node counters next to the value it stores.

images.alt: Three ways to handle concurrent edits. Last-write-wins lets one timestamp decide and silently discards the other change, and clock skew can pick the winner. Version vectors are per-node counters that detect whether two versions are causally ordered or truly concurrent. They only detect conflicts and never merge. CRDTs have a merge that is commutative, associative, and idempotent, so replicas that received the same updates converge in any order. A worked G-Counter merge follows. replicaA holds A 5, B 2, C 0, a value of 7. replicaB holds A 1, B 7, C 4, a value of 12. The element-wise maximum is A 5, B 7, C 4, so the merged value is 16. A closing line notes that converging is not the same as being right.
images.caption: The middle card detects conflicts but doesn't merge them.

options.text: A way to *detect* whether two versions are causally ordered or truly concurrent, but not how to merge them
A guarantee that any two versions can be merged automatically
A synchronized wall-clock time that every node shares
A consensus protocol that elects a single primary writer

questions.explanation:
A version vector records, for each replica, how many of that replica's updates a version includes. Comparing two vectors entry by entry shows how the versions relate. If every entry in A is ≤ the matching entry in B and at least one is strictly smaller, A **happened before** B, and B is the newer version. If neither vector dominates the other, the versions are **concurrent**, which is a real conflict.

So a version vector **detects** conflicts. It doesn't resolve them. Dynamo-style stores return concurrent versions as *siblings* and let the application, or an LWW or CRDT policy, reconcile them. A vector clock tells you *that* a conflict exists and which version descends from which. Picking the merged value is a separate decision for the application.

questions.title: Which statements about CRDTs are true?
questions.description: CRDT stands for **Conflict-free Replicated Data Type**. These data structures power collaborative sync without coordination.

images.alt: Three ways to handle concurrent edits. Last-write-wins lets one timestamp decide and silently discards the other change, and clock skew can pick the winner. Version vectors are per-node counters that detect whether two versions are causally ordered or truly concurrent. They only detect conflicts and never merge. CRDTs have a merge that is commutative, associative, and idempotent, so replicas that received the same updates converge in any order. A worked G-Counter merge follows. replicaA holds A 5, B 2, C 0, a value of 7. replicaB holds A 1, B 7, C 4, a value of 12. The element-wise maximum is A 5, B 7, C 4, so the merged value is 16. A closing line notes that converging is not the same as being right.
images.caption: The right card names the three merge properties.

options.text: Replicas that received the same set of updates end up in the same state, whatever order they applied them in
The merge operation is commutative, associative, and idempotent
Replicas must agree through a consensus protocol (such as Raft) before they can merge
Automatic convergence guarantees the merged result is what the user intended

questions.explanation:
A state-based CRDT's merge is a **join on a semilattice**. It is **commutative, associative, and idempotent**, so replicas converge to one state no matter how updates are ordered or duplicated, with **no coordination or consensus**. That is the "conflict-free" in the name, and it's why CRDTs don't need Raft or Paxos.

"Conflict-free" is a promise about **state**, though, and says nothing about **intent**. Every replica ends up identical, but the result may not be what anyone wanted. If two people edit the same stretch of text at once, the merge can interleave their words in a way neither author meant. CRDTs remove manual merging of state, and your app may still need UI for conflicts in meaning.
questions.references: [crdt.tech: introduction and resources on Conflict-free Replicated Data Types](https://crdt.tech/)

questions.title: After the two replicas merge, what value does the G-Counter report?

images.alt: Three ways to handle concurrent edits. Last-write-wins lets one timestamp decide and silently discards the other change, and clock skew can pick the winner. Version vectors are per-node counters that detect whether two versions are causally ordered or truly concurrent. They only detect conflicts and never merge. CRDTs have a merge that is commutative, associative, and idempotent, so replicas that received the same updates converge in any order. A worked G-Counter merge follows. replicaA holds A 5, B 2, C 0, a value of 7. replicaB holds A 1, B 7, C 4, a value of 12. The element-wise maximum is A 5, B 7, C 4, so the merged value is 16. A closing line notes that converging is not the same as being right.
images.caption: Take the element-wise maximum, then sum the row.

questions.explanation:
The merge takes the **maximum** for each node. Each node only ever increases its own entry, so the larger value is always the newer count for that node, and taking the max never loses an increment.

The element-wise max of the two maps:

- `A`: max(5, 1) = 5
- `B`: max(2, 7) = 7
- `C`: max(0, 4) = 4

The merged state is `{ A: 5, B: 7, C: 4 }`, and the value is the sum: **5 + 7 + 4 = 16**. Both replicas now hold the same merged map, so they have converged.

This merge is commutative, associative, and **idempotent** (merging the same state again changes nothing), which is what makes a G-Counter a CRDT. It's also why a G-Counter can never *decrement*. A shrinking entry would break the rule that the max is the newest value. For decrements you need a **PN-Counter**, which pairs a grow-only map of increments with a second grow-only map of decrements and subtracts one sum from the other.
questions.references: [crdt.tech: introduction and resources on Conflict-free Replicated Data Types](https://crdt.tech/)

questions.title: What does `navigator.onLine === true` actually guarantee?
questions.description: Your sync code checks `navigator.onLine` before it decides whether to flush the outbox.

images.alt: Five steps for one offline mutation. First, apply the change optimistically, which means you must handle failure later. Second, queue the mutation locally in IndexedDB, not localStorage, with an idempotency key so a later replay is safe. Third, try to send it and let the request fail honestly. Fourth, if it fails, register a Background Sync tag so the browser replays the request when the connection returns, even after the tab closes. Fifth, if the server rejects it, roll back the optimistic change and tell the user. Four cards follow. A service worker can use only the Cache API and IndexedDB, not localStorage or document.cookie. An IndexedDB transaction commits on its own as soon as it has no pending request, so awaiting an unrelated fetch makes the next add throw TransactionInactiveError. The browser may still evict stored data unless you call navigator.storage.persist(). A true navigator.onLine only means the device has a network interface.
images.caption: A network interface exists, and that's all it tells you.

options.text: Only that the device has *a* network connection, not that your server or the internet is reachable
That a TCP connection to your API server succeeded
That the last `fetch()` returned a 2xx response
That the service worker is active and controls the page

questions.explanation:
`navigator.onLine` only reports whether the browser thinks it has a network link, for example a connected Wi-Fi interface. It returns `true` behind a captive portal, on a LAN with no internet, and while your API is down. Requests fail in all of these cases.

It works as a cheap **negative** signal: `false` reliably means there's no point trying. A `true` never means a request will succeed. Solid offline-first code assumes the network can fail anyway. Send the request, and if it fails, queue it for retry (ideally with Background Sync) instead of checking `onLine` first. Listen to the `online` and `offline` events to react to changes, but always plan for the request itself to fail.
